sentences.text: Diabloceratops was a medium-sized, moderately built quadrupedal herbivore that lived on the ground. It could grow up to an estimated 5.5 meters in length and weighed 1.3 metric tons.
The name Diabloceratops means "devil-horned face", derived from the Spanish word for devil and the Greek term for horned face.

The type specimen consists of a partial skull with part of the lower jaw, where the right side is intact but the left side is weathered. This animal had a pair of very long spikes on its frill, similar to those found in Einiosaurus and Styracosaurus.

Diabloceratops possessed an accessory opening in the skull that is reduced or absent in later, more advanced ceratopsids. Both Diabloceratops and Protoceratopsidae possess a supplementary opening in the skull that tends to reduce or disappear in more advanced ceratopsians.
At the time of its discovery, Diabloceratops was the oldest-known ceratopsid and the first centrosaurine found south of Montana.
The species Diabloceratops eatoni was named and described in 2010 by James Ian Kirkland and Donald DeBlieux. The genus Diabloceratops was established by Kirkland and DeBlieux in 2010.

Only two specimens of Diabloceratops eatoni have been found in the Wahweap Formation in Kane County, Utah. The only known specimen of Diabloceratops eatoni was found in the Last Chance Creek Member of the Wahweap Formation in Kane County, Utah.

The type specimen UMNH VP 16699 was collected by Don DeBlieux in 2002 from intraclastic sandstone deposited during the Campanian stage of the Cretaceous. The holotype specimen UMNH VP 16699 was collected by Don Deblieux in 2002 at the Last Chance Creek locality.
A second specimen, UMNH VP 16704, was discovered in 1998 by Joshua A. Smith and assigned to Diabloceratops in 2010. The second specimen, UMNH VP 16704, was discovered in 1998 by Joshua A. Smith.
Both specimens are currently housed in the collection of the Utah Natural History Museum.

Diabloceratops shared its environment with hadrosaurs, lambeosaurs, ankylosaurs, pachycephalosaurs, and the theropod Lythronax argestes, likely the apex predator. Diabloceratops shared its environment with dinosaurs such as the hadrosaurid Acristavus gagslarsoni, the lambeosaurine Adelolophus hutchisoni, unnamed ankylosaurids and pachycephalosaurs, and the apex predator theropod Lythronax argestes.
Subsequent phylogenetic analyses continue to classify Diabloceratops as a basal centrosaurine. Diabloceratops is a basal genus within the Centrosaurinae subfamily.
The parent group for Diabloceratops is the subfamily Centrosaurinae. Diabloceratops belongs to the family Ceratopsidae. Diabloceratops is classified within the class Ornithischia.
Kirkland noted that Diabloceratops shared characteristics with the more "primitive" Protoceratopsidae.

During the time Diabloceratops lived, the Western Interior Seaway was at its widest extent, nearly isolating southern Laramidia from the rest of North America. The time range for Diabloceratops is the Campanian stage, spanning from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
The habitat of Diabloceratops included lakes, floodplains, and east-flowing rivers. The habitat included lakes, floodplains, and rivers flowing eastward.
Diabloceratops lived at the end of the Cretaceous Period, approximately 79.9 million years ago during the Campanian, in what is now North America.
Some researchers suggest that specimen UMNH VP 16704 is more similar to Machairoceratops, Yehuecauhceratops, and Menefeeceratops than to Diabloceratops due to the fan-shaped end of the squamosal.
